questions.prompt: ED50 refers to the dose that produces:

options.text: A lethal effect in 50% of a population
50% of the maximal therapeutic effect in 50% of a population

questions.explanation: ED50 (median effective dose) is the dose producing a specified effect (often 50% of maximal response) in 50% of the population tested.

questions.prompt: First-pass metabolism of orally administered drugs primarily occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The liver extensively metabolizes many orally administered drugs before they reach systemic circulation -- first-pass (hepatic) metabolism.

questions.prompt: A drug that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Beta blockers (e.g. propranolol) competitively antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors, commonly used in hypertension and arrhythmias.

questions.prompt: Which route of administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely?
questions.explanation: Intravenous administration delivers the drug directly into systemic circulation, avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism.

questions.prompt: Aspirin exerts its anti-inflammatory effect primarily by inhibiting which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis.

questions.prompt: A drug that competes with an agonist for the same receptor binding site, without activating it, is called a:
questions.explanation: A competitive antagonist binds reversibly to the same site as the agonist, and its effect can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration.

questions.prompt: ACE inhibitors are primarily used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation, widely used as antihypertensives.

questions.prompt: The time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to reduce by half is called its:
questions.explanation: Half-life (t1/2) is the time for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%, a key determinant of dosing frequency.
